### Problem: Remove Covered Intervals {#sec-int-p4-b}

::: {.p-statement}
A list `intervals` of $n$ distinct half-open intervals $[a_i, b_i)$ ($1 \le n \le 1000$, $0 \le a_i < b_i \le 10^5$). An interval $[a_i, b_i)$ is **covered** by $[a_j, b_j)$ iff $a_j \le a_i$ and $b_i \le b_j$. Return the number of intervals that are **not covered** by any other interval. (Containment does not depend on whether the ends are open or closed, so nothing below uses the convention.)

Source: [LC 1288 · Remove Covered Intervals](https://leetcode.com/problems/remove-covered-intervals/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}

Example: `[[1,4],[3,6],[2,8]]` → $2$ ($[3,6]$ is inside $[2,8]$). The worked examples below use `[[1,4],[2,3],[3,6],[4,5]]` → $2$ (only $[1,4]$ and $[3,6]$ survive).
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The direct definition ("is there some other interval that contains this one?") is $O(n^2)$, fine for $n \le 1000$; the sort-based form is just as short and scales to $n = 10^5$ and beyond. The insight: **sort by start ascending, and for ties by end descending**. Once in that order, an interval $[a_i, b_i]$ is covered iff some earlier interval had the same or smaller start and a *larger or equal* end — which is equivalent to $b_i \le$ `max_end_so_far`. The tie-break matters: at equal start, sorting end descending puts the widest one first so any narrower same-start interval is correctly marked as covered; sorting end ascending would flag the widest as extending and miss the containment.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Pairwise containment (oracle).** For each $i$, scan every $j \ne i$ and test $a_j \le a_i$ and $b_i \le b_j$. $O(n^2)$, no sort, no tie-break. The oracle.
2. **Sort by (start asc, end desc) + running max-end.** Sort in $O(n\log n)$; walk with `max_end = 0`; keep interval $i$ iff $b_i >$ `max_end`, then update `max_end` to $b_i$. Count keeps. $O(n\log n)$.
3. **Sort by (end asc, start desc) + right-to-left min-start (dual).** Mirror the second form across the axis. Sort by end ascending, tie-break by start *descending* (widest-left at equal end goes last, so a smaller-start interval is the one kept). Scan the sorted list from right to left with `min_start` starting at positive infinity; keep interval $i$ iff $a_i <$ `min_start`. Symmetric $O(n\log n)$.

**Invariant.** Form 2: after processing index $k$, `max_end` is the largest end among intervals $0..k$, all of which have start $\le$ interval $k$'s start (by the primary sort). If interval $k$'s end $>$ `max_end`, no earlier interval contains it. Form 3 is the same statement read from the right end of the axis.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Pairwise containment

::: {.form-next}
For each interval $i$, scan every $j \ne i$ and test whether $j$ contains $i$. Count how many $i$ survive without being contained. $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ extra. Fine for $n \le 1000$; the sort-based forms below are what you write when $n$ grows.

**Worked example.** $[[1,4],[2,3],[3,6],[4,5]]$: $[1,4]$ — no $j$ contains it (keep). $[2,3]$ — $[1,4]$ contains it (drop). $[3,6]$ — no $j$ contains it (keep). $[4,5]$ — $[3,6]$ contains it (drop). Count $=2$.
:::

```{python}

    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("covered", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def covered_pairwise(intervals):
    keep = 0
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(intervals):
        cov = False
        for j, (a2, b2) in enumerate(intervals):
            if i == j:
                continue
            if a2 <= a and b <= b2:
                # LC's convention: for exact duplicates, only the *later* one is
                # considered covered. So an earlier identical interval must not
                # mark this one as covered.
                if (a2, b2) != (a, b) or j < i:
                    cov = True
                    break
        if not cov:
            keep += 1
    return keep
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - brute force oracle
#include <vector>
using namespace std;
int coveredPairwise(const vector<vector<int>>& iv) {
    int keep = 0, n = (int)iv.size();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        bool cov = false;
        for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) {
            if (i == j) continue;
            if (iv[j][0] <= iv[i][0] && iv[i][1] <= iv[j][1]) {
                // duplicate: only later index counts as covered
                if (iv[j] != iv[i] || j < i) { cov = true; break; }
            }
        }
        if (!cov) ++keep;
    }
    return keep;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The inner predicate $a_j \le a_i$ and $b_i \le b_j$ is the *definition* of "covered"; the `j != i` guard prevents an interval from containing itself (which is always true). The judge promises distinct intervals, but the oracle still handles exact duplicates sensibly, so the random tests may produce them: one copy survives, so when $(a_j, b_j) = (a_i, b_i)$ we only mark $i$ as covered if the equal copy $j$ sits at an earlier index. Two nested loops and one boolean.

#### Sort by (start asc, end desc) + running max-end

::: {.form-next}
Sort intervals primarily by start ascending, with ties broken by end *descending* — the widest first at any shared start. Walk once with `max_end = 0`: keep interval $i$ iff $b_i >$ `max_end` (meaning no earlier interval extends as far or further), then update `max_end = max(max_end, b_i)`. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(1)$ extra state.

**Worked example.** Sort $[[1,4],[2,3],[3,6],[4,5]]$ → already correct order. `max_end=0`: $(1,4)$ → $4 > 0$ keep, `max_end=4`. $(2,3)$ → $3 \le 4$ covered. $(3,6)$ → $6 > 4$ keep, `max_end=6`. $(4,5)$ → $5 \le 6$ covered. Count $=2$.
:::

```{python}

    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1288-sweep
def covered_sweep(intervals):
    s = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: (x[0], -x[1]))
    max_end = -1
    keep = 0
    for a, b in s:
        if b > max_end:
            keep += 1
            max_end = b
    return keep

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 8)
    iv = []
    for _ in range(n):
        a = random.randint(0, 15); b = a + random.randint(0, 5)
        iv.append((a, b))
    assert covered_sweep(iv) == covered_pairwise(iv)
assert covered_sweep([[1,4],[2,3],[3,6],[4,5]]) == 2         # the worked example
assert covered_sweep([[1,4],[3,6],[2,8]]) == 2               # LC sample 1
assert covered_sweep([[1,4],[2,3]]) == 1                     # LC sample 2
assert covered_sweep([[1,4],[1,4]]) == 1                     # equal intervals
assert covered_sweep([[1,4],[1,3]]) == 1                     # shared start, tie-break matters
print("covered_sweep OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
int coveredSweep(vector<vector<int>> intervals) {
    sort(intervals.begin(), intervals.end(),
         [](auto& x, auto& y) {
             return x[0] != y[0] ? x[0] < y[0] : x[1] > y[1];
         });
    int max_end = -1, keep = 0;
    for (auto& iv : intervals) {
        if (iv[1] > max_end) { ++keep; max_end = iv[1]; }
    }
    return keep;
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> v{{1,4},{2,3},{3,6},{4,5}};
    coveredSweep(v);
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** The sort lambda's tie-break `x[1] > y[1]` is where the correctness lives. At a shared start, sorting *end ascending* would place $[1,3]$ before $[1,4]$: the walk keeps $[1,3]$ (its end $3 > 0$), then keeps $[1,4]$ too (end $4 > 3$), giving $2$ — but $[1,3]$ is *covered* by $[1,4]$, so the right answer is $1$. Sorting end *descending* first puts $[1,4]$ up front (keep, `max_end=4`), then $[1,3]$ fails the check and is correctly dropped.

#### Sort by (end asc, start desc) + right-to-left min-start (dual)

::: {.form-next}
The mirror of rung 2 across the number line. Sort by end ascending, tie-break by start descending. Scan the list **from right to left** maintaining `min_start` starting at positive infinity; keep interval $i$ iff $a_i <$ `min_start`, then update. Same $O(n\log n)$; a good check that the sweep insight is really about the *interval order*, not the specific "start-left / end-right" convention.

**Worked example.** $[[1,4],[2,3],[3,6],[4,5]]$ sorted by end asc, start desc $= [(2,3),(1,4),(4,5),(3,6)]$. Reverse-scan: $(3,6)$ — $3 < +\infty$ keep, `min_start=3`; $(4,5)$ — $4 \ge 3$ covered; $(1,4)$ — $1 < 3$ keep, `min_start=1`; $(2,3)$ — $2 \ge 1$ covered. Count $=2$.
:::

##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-1288-dual
def covered_dual(intervals):
    s = sorted(intervals, key=lambda x: (x[1], -x[0]))
    min_start = math.inf
    keep = 0
    for a, b in reversed(s):
        if a < min_start:
            keep += 1
            min_start = a
    return keep

for _ in range(300):
    n = random.randint(1, 8)
    iv = []
    for _ in range(n):
        a = random.randint(0, 15); b = a + random.randint(0, 5)
        iv.append((a, b))
    assert covered_dual(iv) == covered_pairwise(iv)
    assert covered_dual(iv) == covered_sweep(iv)
assert covered_dual([[1,4],[2,3],[3,6],[4,5]]) == 2
print("covered_dual OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <climits>
using namespace std;
int coveredDual(vector<vector<int>> intervals) {
    sort(intervals.begin(), intervals.end(),
         [](auto& x, auto& y) {
             return x[1] != y[1] ? x[1] < y[1] : x[0] > y[0];
         });
    int min_start = INT_MAX, keep = 0;
    for (auto it = intervals.rbegin(); it != intervals.rend(); ++it) {
        if ((*it)[0] < min_start) { ++keep; min_start = (*it)[0]; }
    }
    return keep;
}

int main() {
    vector<vector<int>> v{{1,4},{2,3},{3,6},{4,5}};
    coveredDual(v);
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** Notice the tie-break flips again — this time we want start **descending** at equal ends, so the interval reaching furthest left sits *later* in the sorted order, and the reverse-scan sees it *first*. That way, when two intervals share an end, the wider one becomes the running `min_start` and the narrower one is correctly flagged as covered. The `INT_MAX` / `math.inf` initial value is critical: with `min_start = 0` (the array's start) every interval would fail $a_i < 0$ and we'd report zero kept.
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Pairwise** is $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space. **Sweep** and **dual** are $O(n\log n)$ time dominated by the sort, $O(1)$ extra state (or $O(n)$ if the sort itself allocates). For $n \le 1000$ all three pass with margin; the $O(n\log n)$ forms matter when the same test is reused on large inputs, as in the nested-segments practice problem below.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **Duplicate intervals** $[[1,4],[1,4]]$ (excluded by the judge, produced by the stress test): the second's end is not strictly greater than `max_end`, so it counts as covered. Answer $1$, the same as the oracle.
- **Shared start** $[[1,3],[1,4]]$: tie-break end-descending puts $[1,4]$ first; $[1,3]$ has $b = 3 \le$ `max_end=4` and is dropped. Answer $1$.
- **Shared end** $[[1,5],[3,5]]$ in the sweep form: sorted by start, $[1,5]$ first (`max_end=5`), then $[3,5]$ has $b = 5 \le 5$ and is dropped. Answer $1$.
- **All disjoint** $[[1,2],[3,4],[5,6]]$: every $b >$ `max_end` in turn. Answer $3$.
- **Chain of nestings** $[[1,10],[2,9],[3,8],[4,7]]$: only $[1,10]$ kept. Answer $1$.
:::
